## 11.1 From patterns to experiences and explanations {#ch11-s111}


<p>In Chapter 10, we investigated how observations about people’s
behaviour, experiences and preferences can be collected systematically
through activity counts, questionnaires and other quantitative methods.
Imagine that you have conducted a study of how people use different
parts of an urban park. You may have found that a wooded path is used
less frequently than a more open route, or that visitor numbers vary
substantially throughout the day. These observations establish patterns
in park use, but what explains them? Perhaps people avoid the wooded
path because it is difficult to access, because they are uncertain where
it leads, or because they feel uncomfortable in the enclosed vegetation.
Alternatively, the path may simply connect fewer places that visitors
want to reach. Each explanation suggests a different reason for the
observed pattern, with different implications for how the park might be
managed. You might also have conducted a questionnaire investigating
people’s preferences for different forms of vegetation management and
found that many respondents prefer more natural-looking greenery. But
what do they mean by <em>natural</em>? Some may associate it with
spontaneous vegetation growth and greater biodiversity, others with
large trees and comfortable shade, and still others with a landscape
that looks relatively undisturbed but remains carefully maintained.
Respondents giving the same answer may therefore have rather different
environments in mind. The survey results can provide valuable
information about the distribution of reported preferences, but
understanding what those preferences involve, how they develop and how
they might influence people’s behaviour requires us to investigate these
differences more closely. We could do so by talking with park users
about their experiences, asking them to describe particular locations or
accompanying them as they walk through the park. Their explanations
might reveal influences on park use that we had not considered when
designing our original study. For example, we might discover that some
visitors avoid the wooded path not because they dislike dense vegetation
but because they cannot see where the path leads. Others may appreciate
the shaded environment but find its uneven surface difficult to
negotiate. We could compare these accounts with our own observations,
investigate whether other visitors describe similar experiences, and
examine whether the proposed explanations are consistent with the
physical characteristics and observed use of the locations. These accounts give us several possible explanations to examine against the observations and the settings in which people make their choices.</p>
<p>To assess those explanations, we also need to consider how the accounts were produced: the questions asked, the circumstances described and the experiences participants bring to the conversation. If we ask only frequent park users, we will learn relatively little about those who rarely visit. If we ask whether the wooded route is “safe”, one participant may think about traffic, another about visibility at dusk and another about the likelihood of meeting unfamiliar people. We need to retain the wording and setting of each account, compare experiences across relevant groups and places, and examine interpretations against other observations. This connects directly with the system understanding developed in Chapter 2: interviews and observation can reveal a relationship we did not initially include, suggest why a measured pattern differs among people, or lead us to measure something new. A quantitative finding can likewise generate a question that we follow up through qualitative research. Consider, for example, two visitors who both give the wooded path a low comfort rating. One finds that it requires a long detour from a bus stop. The other avoids enclosed vegetation at dusk because they cannot see who might be approaching. The numerical responses are identical, but the accounts suggest different processes and, potentially, different responses from park managers. If we subsequently want to estimate how common each concern is, we need to define the population of interest, select respondents accordingly and ask questions that distinguish those experiences. Interviews can thus change both the explanation we are considering and what needs to be sampled or measured to investigate it.</p>

<section class="ch11-exercise" id="ch11-exercise-1"><h4>Test your understanding 11.1 · Match the claim to the evidence</h4><div class="ch11-question"><p>Choose a suitable primary approach for each question: (i) What
fraction of nearby residents support reduced mowing? (ii) Why do some
visitors describe wooded areas as peaceful while others describe them as
unsafe? (iii) How do maintenance staff decide which informal paths to
clear? (iv) How have residents’ memories of a mangrove area changed
across generations? For each, identify a possible unit of inquiry and
what the method would record. Explain when interviews could complement,
but not replace, a population survey.</p></div><label for="ch11-exercise-1-answer">Your reasoning</label><textarea id="ch11-exercise-1-answer" placeholder="Write a short explanation before revealing the suggested response." rows="4"></textarea><div class="ch11-actions"><span aria-live="polite" class="ch11-count">0 words</span><button aria-expanded="false" class="ch11-reveal" disabled="" type="button">Show suggested response</button></div><div class="ch11-solution" hidden=""><p>For (i), the quantity sought is the proportion of *nearby residents* who support reduced mowing. A defined residential population and a survey sampling strategy are needed if the result is to be used as an estimate for that population. The unit is an eligible resident, or perhaps a household if the question is explicitly about households; a questionnaire would record an operationally defined response, ideally after piloting what “reduced mowing” means. Interviews with a smaller, deliberately varied group could help us understand what residents imagine when they hear the term, including whether it implies wildflowers, untidiness, pests or a loss of play space. They would improve the survey questions but could not by themselves establish the population percentage. For (ii), we need to understand different interpretations of the same wooded setting. The primary units could be individual visits and participants' accounts of those visits. Semi-structured interviews, preferably with a walk through the site for some participants, would explore when and where the experience occurred, what features participants noticed, and whether darkness, visibility, previous incidents or companions shaped the assessment. Observations and measurements of route conditions might help test interpretations, but a reported feeling of insecurity is not itself a measurement of actual risk. For (iii), maintenance *decisions and practices* are the focus. Interviews with staff can elicit stated responsibilities and criteria; observation of maintenance work and examination of work orders can show how decisions are implemented under constraints of staffing, safety and institutional rules. The unit might be a clearing decision or maintenance episode, not merely a staff member. Official policies alone may not explain day-to-day decisions. For (iv), oral-history interviews with people who knew the mangrove at different stages, together with dated photographs, maps and archival records, can reconstruct remembered uses and environmental changes. Here the units include individual recollections, documentary records and identifiable historical events. Memories from different age groups are not a repeated population survey, so a change in the accounts does not automatically demonstrate a shift in the prevalence of values across generations. In all four cases, a different approach could be appropriate if we changed the claim we wanted to make: the method must be chosen to produce evidence for that claim, not simply because the topic concerns people.</p></div><noscript><details><summary>Suggested response (available without JavaScript)</summary><p>For (i), the quantity sought is the proportion of *nearby residents* who support reduced mowing. ## 11.2 Interviews {#ch11-s112}


<p>You probably have a reasonable idea of what an interview involves,
even if you have never conducted one yourself. We ask someone questions
about a particular subject, listen to their answers and often ask
further questions to understand what they mean. In research, however, we
want to use those conversations to answer specific questions about the
system we are studying. This requires some preparation. We need to
consider whom to interview, what we want to learn from them, how to
formulate questions that allow them to explain their experiences, and
how we will record and subsequently interpret their answers. The person
being interviewed brings their own knowledge, memories, experiences and
interests, but the interviewer also influences the conversation through
the questions asked, the order in which topics are introduced and the
way responses are followed up. For example, asking someone whether they
avoid a wooded path because they feel unsafe may lead to a quite
different conversation from asking them to describe how they decide
which route to take through the park. The interview questions and the way they are followed up therefore influence which experiences and explanations become part of the research record.</p>
<p>There are different ways of organising interviews, depending on what
we want to investigate. A <strong>structured interview</strong> follows
a largely predetermined set of questions, often with standardised
response options. This makes it easier to compare answers across many
participants and is similar to an interviewer-administered
questionnaire. A <strong>semi-structured interview</strong> also uses a
prepared set of questions or topics, but allows the interviewer to
change their sequence, ask additional questions and follow up on
unexpected information. For example, we might want to discuss park use,
accessibility, comfort and vegetation preferences with every
participant, while leaving room for each person to describe experiences
that we had not anticipated. In a more <strong>open or narrative
interview</strong>, the participant has greater freedom to decide what
to discuss and how to organise their account. We might ask someone who
has lived near a coastal park for several decades to describe how the
area and its uses have changed during their lifetime, allowing them to
identify events and experiences that they consider important. These
approaches are not entirely separate categories. Interviews can differ
in how closely they follow predetermined questions, how much freedom
participants have to introduce new topics, and how extensively
particular experiences are explored. Preparing an interview guide then requires deciding how much structure is useful and where participants need room to introduce experiences or explanations we have not anticipated.</p>
<p>Designing and conducting an interview that provides useful evidence
is not necessarily straightforward. We usually want enough consistency
across interviews to compare what different people tell us, while also
allowing individual participants to explain their experiences in their
own terms. Consider again our investigation of how people use different
parts of an urban park. We might begin by asking someone to describe
their most recent visit: where they went, which places they stopped at
and what influenced their choices. This provides a concrete starting
point, and the interviewer can then ask further questions about
particular decisions or experiences. If the participant mentions that
they avoided a wooded path, we could ask what made them decide against
using it. Perhaps they did not know where it led, found it difficult to
walk on, or were simply going somewhere else. We would learn rather less
by immediately asking, ‘Do you avoid the wooded path because it feels
unsafe?’ That question assumes that they avoid the path and introduces a
particular explanation before we know whether it is relevant. Similarly,
asking whether someone prefers shaded areas may tell us something about
their stated preference, but asking them to describe where they went
during a recent visit may reveal how shade influences their choices in
relation to other considerations, such as accessibility, destinations or
the activities they intended to undertake. We can still ask directly
about shade later in the interview, particularly if it is important to
our research question. The point is to give participants an opportunity
to describe their experiences before we introduce all our own possible
explanations. When preparing an interview, we therefore need to think not only
about the questions we intend to ask, but also about how the
conversation might develop. In a semi-structured interview, an interview
guide can identify the main topics that should be discussed with every
participant, together with possible follow-up questions. For the park
study, we might include questions about recent visits, commonly used
routes, places people particularly appreciate or avoid, and how their
use of the park varies with time of day or weather. Within each topic,
we can prepare prompts that help participants provide more detail: when
did something happen, what were the circumstances, who was involved, and
has their experience changed over time? At the same time, we need to
listen carefully enough to recognise when an answer introduces something
we had not considered. Someone may unexpectedly mention that they no
longer visit a particular area because maintenance activities have
changed the paths, or that their preferences differ depending on whether
they come alone or with children. These observations may suggest
additional questions worth asking other participants, or new
relationships to consider in our understanding of the park. We should
therefore test the interview guide before using it for the main study. A
few pilot interviews can reveal questions that are difficult to
understand, terms that different people interpret differently, or topics
that are important to participants but missing from our guide. They also
help us practise following up on answers without repeatedly directing
participants towards explanations we already have in mind.</p>

<p>As with other field methods, the circumstances in which interviews
are conducted affect the information we collect. Interviewing someone
beside a busy path may be convenient, but background noise,
interruptions or the presence of other people may make it difficult for
them to explain their experiences freely. An interview conducted in a
quiet and comfortable location may allow a more extensive conversation,
although it may also be less convenient for some participants. Language
is another consideration. People may be better able to explain their
experiences in a language with which they are familiar, and translation
may be necessary when the researcher and participant do not share that
language. We also need to decide how to record the interview. With
appropriate consent, an audio recording can preserve much of what was
said and allow the interviewer to concentrate on the conversation.
Recordings can be transcribed manually or with software, including
automated transcription tools, but the resulting transcripts need to be
checked because names, unfamiliar terms, accents and overlapping speech
can produce errors. Field notes remain useful even when recordings are
available. They can document the location and circumstances of the
interview, relevant observations that are not captured in the audio,
interruptions, and questions that arose during the conversation. These
details can become important when interpreting a participant’s account.
For example, someone’s statement that a park location is ‘usually quiet’
may need to be understood in relation to when they normally visit,
particularly if the interviewer has observed quite different conditions
at other times.</p>
<p>People’s experiences, willingness
to participate and ways of explaining themselves vary considerably. Two
people who regularly visit the same park may use it for different
purposes and encounter different conditions. Their experiences may also
depend on age, mobility, familiarity with the park, the activities they
undertake and the times at which they visit. Some of this variation is
precisely what we want to understand. But the circumstances of
recruitment and interviewing can introduce additional differences. Some
people may be comfortable discussing their experiences with a university
researcher, while others may be reluctant, unsure why the information is
being collected or concerned about possible consequences of what they
say. Someone approached through a park authority may respond differently
from someone recruited independently. We should be aware of these
influences when interpreting similarities and differences among
interviews. Where possible, the sampling design can deliberately include
people with contrasting experiences, while our interview records should
help us understand the circumstances under which different accounts were
obtained. We cannot anticipate or control every influence, nor can we
assume that speaking with several people from the same nominal group
adequately captures the variation within it. This connects to the
principles of sampling and variability discussed earlier in the book: we
need to consider which differences are relevant to our research
question, which our design allows us to investigate, and which may
remain poorly represented. The next section develops how participants
can be selected to explore such variation, including experiences and
perspectives that would be difficult to reach through a survey of
current park users alone. For fuller treatment of how interview
questions, relationships and transcription influence the evidence, see
@brinkmannkvale2014.</p>
<details class="ch11-foldable box" id="ch11-note-2"><summary>Box 11.1 · An interview-guide prototype for park experience</summary><div class="ch11-foldable-body"><p><strong>Research purpose.</strong> Understand why visitors choose or
avoid differently managed park settings and what they mean by comfort or
naturalness. <strong>Eligibility.</strong> People with relevant recent
experience; the broader question may also require a separate group of
non-visitors.</p>
<p><strong>Opening.</strong> ‘Can you tell me about a recent visit to
this park? Where did you go, and what did you do?’ Allow the account to
develop before asking for reasons.</p>
<p><strong>Probe for choices.</strong> ‘What influenced your route?’
‘Were there places you chose not to use?’ ‘How does that compare with
other visits?’ Ask for examples if the account remains abstract.</p>
<p><strong>Probe for interpretation.</strong> ‘You described that area
as natural. What made it feel natural to you?’ ‘Would another part of
the park fit that description?’ Avoid presupposing that one meaning is
scientifically correct.</p>
<p><strong>Probe for management change.</strong> ‘Have you noticed
changes in the vegetation or maintenance?’ ‘What difference, if any,
have those changes made to your experience?’ The respondent may not have
noticed a change; do not push for a causal story.</p>
<p><strong>Closing.</strong> ‘Is there something important about your
use of the park that my questions have not covered?’ Document the
setting, date, conditions and any analytic memo without unnecessarily
recording identifiable details.</p>
<p><strong>Quality check.</strong> Does each question invite an account?
Is it understandable without specialist vocabulary? Is the interview
long enough to develop examples, yet short enough to respect
participants’ time? Are consent and permissions in place?</p><p><strong>Further reading.</strong> @brinkmannkvale2014 provide a specialist account of interview design, follow-up questioning and the interpretation of what interview conversations produce.</p></div></details>
<details class="ch11-foldable box" id="ch11-textbooks-for-methods"><summary>Box 11.2 · Books for developing qualitative field methods</summary><div class="ch11-foldable-body">
<p><strong>@newing2011, <em>Conducting Research in Conservation</em>.</strong> A practical introduction to social-science approaches in environmental and conservation projects, including interviewing, sampling, field procedures and the decisions that connect methods to research questions.</p>
<p><strong>@hammersley2019, <em>Ethnography: Principles in Practice</em>.</strong> Explains how extended observation, interviews and documentary material are used together, how field relationships shape information, and how researchers move from descriptive records to interpretations.</p>
<p><strong>@brinkmannkvale2014, <em>InterViews</em>.</strong> Develops the craft of designing, conducting, interpreting and reporting research interviews, with more attention to interviewing practice than a short methods chapter can provide.</p>
</div></details>
